title: a house built on five
hookLine: not a checklist: a building, and the building is made of time
carry: five things that hold a life up

cards: The five pillars of Islam often get learned like a list for a test. Witness. Prayer.
Five boxes, done. Said that way, it sounds like a checklist. But the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ didn't describe them as a list.
He described them as a building. And the building turns out to be made of time.

teach.b: Islam is built on five, a saying of the Prophet goes. Built, like a house; pillars are what keep the roof up. One: the shahada, the witness.

There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God. One sentence, said to become Muslim and said inside every prayer, the same sentence whether you've said it since childhood or for the first time last month.
Its clock is always. Two: salat, prayer, five times a day, at times that move with the sun. Its clock is the day.
Three: zakat, giving a set share of savings to people in need, once a year. Four: sawm, the Ramadan fast you met on day six. Their clock is the year.
Five: hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca, once in a lifetime. Its clock is a life. Now look at the shape.
Once in a life. Circles inside circles.
And the house fits the person living in it: the Qur'an lets the sick and the traveler make up missed fast days, and asks for the hajj only from those able to make the journey.
Muslims also draw the house in more than one way. Sunni teaching usually names these five as the pillars.

teach.h: ROOTS AND BRANCHES: DRAWN TWO WAYS.
teach.b: Shia teaching usually speaks of roots, the core beliefs, and branches, the practices: the witness lives in the roots, and prayer, fasting, giving and pilgrimage among the branches. Same house, drawn two ways.

how: Muslims keep the five together: the shahada as the core of faith, the five daily prayers, zakat given yearly, the Ramadan fast, and the hajj once in a lifetime for those able. Shia Muslims keep the same practices and describe the faith as roots (beliefs) and branches (practices).

games.q: put each pillar on its clock — tap the pairs.
p: pilgrimage: once in a life, if able

s: every Muslim must make the hajj, no matter what
the Qur'an asks it of those able to make the journey (3:97).
the prayer times move with the sun
dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset, night: the clock is the sky.
Shia teaching draws the faith as roots and branches
roots are the core beliefs; prayer, fasting, giving and pilgrimage are among the branches.

games.q: it's Ramadan, and you're sick. what does the Qur'an say about the fast?
o: the sick may make up those days later.
the whole month no longer counts.
games.why: the sick and the traveler make up the missed days later (2:184). the house is built to fit the person living in it.

practice: Sit comfortably. The pillars are circles of time, so borrow the shape. Bring to mind something that holds up your day, and let it stay a moment.
Then something that holds up your year. Then something you'd want to do once in your life. Nothing to do about any of them.
Just see what's holding you up.

wordCard.voice: The five pillars. Witness, prayer, giving, fasting, pilgrimage: not five boxes but a house built on five. Ninth word.

orig.note: Arabic: "the pillars of Islam." arkan is the plural of rukn, a pillar or supporting corner.

carryVoice: Your line: five things that hold a life up. Always, daily, yearly, once. Day nine.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 8; Sahih Muslim 16 (Islam is built on five)
Shia teaching: usul al-din and furu' al-din (roots and branches of religion)
